claim: All membrane fusion reactions proceed through an initial fusion pore, including calcium-triggered release of neurotransmitters and hormones.
source: All membrane fusion reactions proceed through an initial fusion pore, including calcium-triggered release of neurotransmitters and hormones.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about membrane fusion processes.

claim: Expansion of the fusion pore to release cargo is energetically costly and regulated by cells.
source: Expansion of this small pore to release cargo is energetically costly and regulated by cells, but the mechanisms are poorly understood.
evidence: This statement draws from established understanding in the field about fusion pore energetics.

claim: The neuronal/exocytic calcium sensor Synaptotagmin-1 (Syt1) promotes expansion of fusion pores induced by SNARE proteins.
source: Here, we show that the neuronal/exocytic calcium sensor Synaptotagmin-1 (Syt1) promotes expansion of fusion pores induced by SNARE proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pore dilation by Syt1 relied on calcium-induced insertion of the tandem C2 domain hydrophobic loops into the membrane.
source: Pore dilation relied on calcium-induced insertion of the tandem C2 domain hydrophobic loops of Syt1 into the membrane, previously shown to reorient the C2 domain.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with mutants and by citations to previous work on C2 domain reorientation.

claim: Mathematical modelling suggests that C2B reorientation rotates a bound SNARE complex so that it exerts force on the membranes in a mechanical lever action that increases the height of the fusion pore.
source: Mathematical modelling suggests that C2B reorientation rotates a bound SNARE complex so that it exerts force on the membranes in a mechanical lever action that increases the height of the fusion pore, provoking pore dilation to offset the bending energy penalty.
evidence: This is based on mathematical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Syt1 exerts novel non-local calcium-dependent mechanical forces on fusion pores that dilate pores and assist neurotransmitter and hormone release.
source: We conclude that Syt1 exerts novel non-local calcium-dependent mechanical forces on fusion pores that dilate pores and assist neurotransmitter and hormone release.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and modeling presented in the study.

claim: The initial merger of the vesicular and plasma membranes results in a narrow fusion pore only ~1 nm in diameter.
source: The initial merger of the vesicular and plasma membranes results in a narrow fusion pore only ~1 nm in diameter (Karatekin, 2018; Sharma and Lindau, 2018; Chang et al., 2017; Alabi and Tsien, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The fusion pore can fluctuate in size, flicker open-closed multiple times and either reseal after partial release of contents or dilate for full cargo release.
source: The fusion pore can fluctuate in size, flicker open-closed multiple times and either reseal after partial release of contents or dilate for full cargo release.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fusion pore dynamics.

claim: In pancreatic β-cells, fusion pores that fail to dilate release only small cargo such as ATP, but not insulin, a process that occurs more commonly in type 2 diabetes.
source: In pancreatic β-cells, fusion pores that fail to dilate release only small cargo such as ATP, but not insulin, a process that occurs more commonly in type 2 diabetes (Collins et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Adrenal chromaffin cells release small catecholamines through flickering small pores, or release additional, larger cargo, in an activity-dependent manner.
source: Adrenal chromaffin cells release small catecholamines through flickering small pores, or release additional, larger cargo, in an activity-dependent manner (Fulop et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: SNARE proteins are a core component of the release machinery and are known to influence fusion pore dynamics.
source: SNARE proteins, a core component of the release machinery, are known to influence fusion pore dynamics (Bao et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2017b; Wu et al., 2017a; Han et al., 2004; Bretou et al., 2008; Kesavan et al., 2007; Dhara et al., 2016; Ngatchou et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Formation of complexes between the vesicular v-SNARE VAMP2/Syb2 and plasma membrane t-SNAREs Syntaxin-1/SNAP25 is required for fusion.
source: Formation of complexes between the vesicular v-SNARE VAMP2/Syb2 and plasma membrane t-SNAREs Syntaxin-1/SNAP25 is required for fusion (Weber et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Insertion of flexible linkers between the SNARE domain and the transmembrane domain in VAMP2, or truncation of the last nine residues of SNAP25, retard fusion pore expansion in adrenal chromaffin cells.
source: Insertion of flexible linkers between the SNARE domain and the transmembrane domain in VAMP2, or truncation of the last nine residues of SNAP25, retard fusion pore expansion in adrenal chromaffin cells (Bretou et al., 2008; Kesavan et al., 2007; Fang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mutations in SNARE TMDs affect fusion pores.
source: Mutations in SNARE TMDs also affect fusion pores (Wu et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Increasing the number of SNAREs at the fusion site accelerated fusion pore expansion in neurons, astrocytes, and chromaffin cells.
source: Increasing the number of SNAREs at the fusion site accelerated fusion pore expansion in neurons (Bao et al., 2018; Acuna et al., 2014), astrocytes (Guček et al., 2016), and chromaffin cells (Zhao et al., 2013) and led to larger pores in nanodisc-based single-pore fusion assays (Bao et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Increased SNARE copy numbers were interpreted as due to increased molecular crowding at the waist of the pore.
source: This was interpreted as due to increased molecular crowding at the waist of the pore with increasing SNARE copy numbers (Wu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is an interpretation from a cited previous work.

claim: Synaptotagmins are another component of the release machinery known to affect fusion pore properties.
source: Although they are best known for their role as calcium sensors for exocytosis at most synapses and endocrine cells, Synaptotagmins are another component of the release machinery known to affect fusion pore properties (Segovia et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010a; Zhang et al., 2010b; Wang et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2003a; Wang et al., 2003b; Wang et al., 2001; Bai et al., 2004a; Lynch et al., 2008; Rao et al., 2014; Lai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Synaptotagmins couple membrane fusion driven by neuronal/exocytic SNAREs to calcium influx.
source: They couple membrane fusion driven by neuronal/exocytic SNAREs to calcium influx (Geppert et al., 1994; Chapman, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Synaptotagmins are integral membrane proteins possessing two cytosolic C2 domains (C2A and C2B) which can bind Ca2+, acidic lipids, SNAREs, and other effectors.
source: Synaptotagmins are integral membrane proteins possessing two cytosolic C2 domains (C2A and C2B) which can bind Ca2+, acidic lipids, SNAREs, and other effectors, but affinities vary widely among the 17 mammalian isoforms (Chapman, 2008; Bhalla et al., 2005; Bhalla et al., 2008; Pinheiro et al., 2016; Volynski and Krishnakumar, 2018; Craxton, 2010; Sugita et al., 2002; Hui et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Synaptotagmin-1 (Syt1) is the major neuronal isoform that mediates fast, synchronous neurotransmitter release.
source: Synaptotagmin-1 (Syt1) is the major neuronal isoform that mediates fast, synchronous neurotransmitter release (Chapman, 2008; Volynski and Krishnakumar, 2018; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Syt1 resides in synaptic vesicles in neurons and secretory granules in neuroendocrine cells and interacts with SNAREs, acidic phospholipids, and calcium.
source: It resides in synaptic vesicles in neurons and secretory granules in neuroendocrine cells and interacts with SNAREs, acidic phospholipids, and calcium (Brunger et al., 2018a; Chapman, 2008; Brunger et al., 2018b; Südhof, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Calcium-binding to Syt1 causes hydrophobic residues at the tips of the Ca2+-binding loops to insert into the membrane, generating curvature.
source: Calcium-binding to Syt1 causes hydrophobic residues at the tips of the Ca2+-binding loops to insert into the membrane, generating curvature, which may be important for triggering fusion (Lynch et al., 2008; Martens et al., 2007; Hui et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Membrane bending has been proposed to facilitate opening of the initial fusion pore by helping to bring the two membranes into close proximity, reducing the repulsive hydration forces by reducing the contact area, and exposing the hydrophobic interior of the two membranes to initiate lipid exchange.
source: Membrane bending has been proposed to facilitate opening of the initial fusion pore by helping to bring the two membranes into close proximity, reducing the repulsive hydration forces by reducing the contact area, and exposing the hydrophobic interior of the two membranes to initiate lipid exchange (Chernomordik and Kozlov, 2008; Kozlov et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In PC12 cells, membrane-insertion deficient mutants reduced exocytosis, whereas mutants with enhanced insertion led to larger fusion pores.
source: After fusion pore opening, Syt1 was suggested to contribute to fusion pore expansion through membrane curvature generation as well, based on the observation that in PC12 cells, membrane-insertion deficient mutants reduced exocytosis, whereas mutants with enhanced insertion led to larger fusion pores (Lynch et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In adrenal chromaffin cells where Syt1 and Syt7 are sorted to distinct granule populations, fusion pores of Syt7 granules dilate more slowly.
source: In adrenal chromaffin cells where Syt1 and Syt7 are sorted to distinct granule populations, fusion pores of Syt7 granules dilate more slowly (Rao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Compared to Syt1 C2 domains, the higher calcium-affinity Syt7 C2 domains penetrate more avidly and deeply into membranes.
source: Second, compared to Syt1 C2 domains, the higher calcium-affinity Syt7 C2 domains penetrate more avidly and deeply into membranes (Osterberg et al., 2015; Voleti et al., 2017), which should lead to more efficient membrane bending (Martens et al., 2007; Hui et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ~4 copies of recombinant full-length Syt1 together with ~4 copies of VAMP2 (per disc face) were co-reconstituted into large nanodiscs called nanolipoprotein particles.
source: To test whether Syt1 affected fusion pores in this system, we co-reconstituted ~4 copies of recombinant full-length Syt1 together with ~4 copies of VAMP2 (per disc face) into large nanodiscs called nanolipoprotein particles (Wu et al., 2017b; Bello et al., 2016) (vsNLPs, ~25 nm in diameter, see Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Only ~2 SNARE complexes are sufficient to open a small fusion pore (150-200 pS conductance).
source: In the absence of Syt1, we previously found that only ~2 SNARE complexes are sufficient to open a small fusion pore (150-200 pS conductance), but dilation of the pore beyond ~1 nS conductance (~1.7 nm in radius, assuming the pore is a 15 nm long cylinder [Hille, 2001]) required the cooperative action of more than ~10 SNARE complexes (Wu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors.

claim: Dilation of the pore beyond ~1 nS conductance (~1.7 nm in radius) required the cooperative action of more than ~10 SNARE complexes.
source: In the absence of Syt1, we previously found that only ~2 SNARE complexes are sufficient to open a small fusion pore (150-200 pS conductance), but dilation of the pore beyond ~1 nS conductance (~1.7 nm in radius, assuming the pore is a 15 nm long cylinder [Hille, 2001]) required the cooperative action of more than ~10 SNARE complexes (Wu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors.

claim: With ~4 v-SNAREs per NLP face, fusion driven by SNAREs alone results in relatively small pores with ~200 pS average conductance, corresponding to a pore radius of ~0.76 nm.
source: With ~4 v-SNAREs per NLP face, fusion driven by SNAREs alone results in relatively small pores with ~200 pS average conductance, corresponding to a pore radius of ~0.76 nm (Wu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors.

claim: The distribution of NLP diameters was fairly narrow, with mean diameter 25 nm (±5.6 nm SD).
source: The distribution of NLP diameters was fairly narrow, with mean diameter 25 nm (±5.6 nm SD, see Appendix 1—figure 1E), and did not change significantly compared to the distribution when v-SNAREs alone were incorporated at ~4 copies per face (mean diameter = 25 ± 4 nm) (see Appendix 1—figure 1F-H, and Wu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 1E.

claim: Even in the presence of 100 μM free calcium, pore properties were affected only slightly compared to the case when Syt1 was omitted from the NLPs when exogenous PI(4,5)P2 was not added.
source: Even in the presence of 100 μM free calcium, a level that elicits robust release in neurons and chromaffin cells (Pinheiro et al., 2016; Schneggenburger and Neher, 2000; Schneggenburger and Neher, 2005; Voets, 2000; Chanaday and Kavalali, 2018), pore properties were affected only slightly compared to the case when Syt1 was omitted from the NLPs.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Syt1 is known to interact with acidic lipids, in particular with PI(4,5)P2, in both calcium-dependent and independent manners, and these interactions are required for Syt1's ability to trigger membrane fusion.
source: Syt1 is known to interact with acidic lipids, in particular with PI(4,5)P2, in both calcium-dependent and independent manners, and these interactions are required for Syt1's ability to trigger membrane fusion (Zhang et al., 2010a; Chang et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2017; Pérez-Lara et al., 2016; Honigmann et al., 2013; Bai et al., 2004b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Outer leaflet diC8PI(4,5)P2 levels were within 25% of the endogenous inner-leaflet PI(4,5)P2 levels.
source: Outer leaflet diC8PI(4,5)P2 levels were within 25% of the endogenous inner-leaflet PI(4,5)P2 levels (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: When vsNLP-flipped t-SNARE cell fusion experiments were repeated with cells pre-incubated with diC8PI(4,5)P2, the rate of fusion in the absence of calcium was unchanged compared to fusion with SNAREs alone, but increased three- to fourfold when 100 μM calcium was present.
source: When we repeated vsNLP-flipped t-SNARE cell fusion experiments with cells pre-incubated with diC8PI(4,5)P2, the rate of fusion in the absence of calcium was unchanged compared to fusion with SNAREs alone, but increased three- to fourfold when 100 μM calcium was present (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Compared to SNARE-alone fusion, the mean single-pore conductance increased only slightly in the absence of calcium but was three-fold larger in the presence of 100 μM calcium.
source: Compared to SNARE-alone fusion, the mean single-pore conductance increased only slightly in the absence of calcium but was three-fold larger in the presence of 100 μM calcium (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Treatment with the tetanus neurotoxin TeNT, which cleaves VAMP2 at position 76Q-77F and blocks exocytosis, dramatically reduced the fusion rate of vsNLPs even in the presence of calcium and exogenous PI(4,5)P2.
source: Fusion was SNARE-dependent, as treatment with the tetanus neurotoxin TeNT, which cleaves VAMP2 at position 76Q-77F and blocks exocytosis (Schiavo et al., 2000), dramatically reduced the fusion rate of vsNLPs even in the presence of calcium and exogenous PI(4,5)P2 (Figure 1D and Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 2A, and by a citation about TeNT function.

claim: Syt1 increases the fusion rate and promotes pore dilation during SNARE-induced fusion, in a calcium- and PI(4,5)P2-dependent manner.
source: Thus, Syt1 increases the fusion rate and promotes pore dilation during SNARE-induced fusion, in a calcium- and PI(4,5)P2-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: In the presence of 100 μM free calcium and exogenous PI(4,5)P2, larger conductance values (and corresponding pore radii) became more likely.
source: By contrast, in the presence of 100 μM free calcium and exogenous PI(4,5)P2, larger conductance values (and corresponding pore radii) became more likely (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: With SNAREs alone, or with Syt1 but in the absence of calcium, ~6-7 kT energy was required to expand the pore from 1 to ~2.5 nm radius.
source: With SNAREs alone, or with Syt1 but in the absence of calcium, the free energy profile suggested that ~6-7 kT energy was required to expand the pore from 1 to ~2.5 nm radius, whereas calcium-bound Syt1 reduced this resistance to ~2 kT (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Calcium-bound Syt1 reduced the energy required to expand the pore from 1 to ~2.5 nm radius to ~2 kT.
source: With SNAREs alone, or with Syt1 but in the absence of calcium, the free energy profile suggested that ~6-7 kT energy was required to expand the pore from 1 to ~2.5 nm radius, whereas calcium-bound Syt1 reduced this resistance to ~2 kT (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The force opposing pore expansion decreased from 16-19 pN in the absence of calcium to ~5 pN in the presence of 100 μM calcium.
source: That is, the force opposing pore expansion decreased from 16-19 pN in the absence of calcium to ~5 pN in the presence of 100 μM calcium.
evidence: This is calculated from the free energy profiles derived from experimental data.

claim: Soluble C2AB largely recapitulates the effect of full-length Syt1 on promoting dilation of SNARE-mediated fusion pores.
source: We conclude that soluble Syt1 C2AB largely recapitulates the effect of full-length Syt1 on promoting dilation of SNARE-mediated fusion pores.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing experimental results with full-length Syt1 and soluble C2AB.

claim: Binding of calcium to the second C2 domain of Syt1 is known to be essential for evoked release.
source: Binding of calcium to the second C2 domain of Syt1 is known to be essential for evoked release (Chapman, 2008; Mackler et al., 2002; Shin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: When calcium binding to the C2B domain was impaired by mutating a highly conserved aspartate to asparagine (Syt1 C2AB D309N), mean single pore conductance returned to the value obtained in the presence of SNAREs alone.
source: When calcium binding to the C2B domain was impaired by mutating a highly conserved aspartate to asparagine (Syt1 C2AB D309N Nishiki and Augustine, 2004), mean single pore conductance returned to the value obtained in the presence of SNAREs alone (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Calcium binding to Syt1 C2B is essential for fusion pore dilation, in addition to its well-known role for triggering the opening of a fusion pore.
source: We conclude that calcium binding to Syt1 C2B is essential for fusion pore dilation, in addition to its well-known role for triggering the opening of a fusion pore (Wang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with the D309N mutant.

claim: The C2B domain of Syt1 possesses a polybasic patch (K324-327) that interacts with acidic phospholipids and is important for synchronous evoked release.
source: The C2B domain of Syt1 possesses a polybasic patch (K324-327) that interacts with acidic phospholipids (Figure 3A) and is important for synchronous evoked release (Chang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Partially neutralizing the polybasic patch in C2B (K326A, K327A) reduced the fusion rate, and resulted in single pore conductances that were indistinguishable from those for SNARE-alone pores.
source: Partially neutralizing the polybasic patch in C2B (K326A, K327A) reduced the fusion rate, and resulted in single pore conductances that were indistinguishable from those for SNARE-alone pores (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The polybasic patch in Syt1 C2B is required for fusion pore dilation.
source: Thus, in addition to its established role in evoked release (Chang et al., 2018; Borden et al., 2005), the polybasic patch in Syt1 C2B is also required for fusion pore dilation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with the K326A, K327A mutant.

claim: Two arginines (R398 and R399) in Syt1 C2B form salt bridges with glutamates and aspartates in a groove between SNAP25 and Syntaxin-1.
source: Specifically, two arginines (R398 and R399) form salt bridges with glutamates and aspartates in a groove between SNAP25 and Syntaxin-1 (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous structural work.

claim: Mutation of R398 and R399 to glutamines (R398Q, R399Q) was shown to largely abolish evoked release from hippocampal neurons.
source: Mutation of these arginines to glutamines (R398Q, R399Q) was shown to largely abolish evoked release from hippocampal neurons (Chang et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2015; Xue et al., 2008), possibly by disrupting the interaction of Syt1 C2B with SNAREs (Chang et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: When C2ABR398Q, R399Q mutant was used, both the fusion rate and the mean pore conductance decreased significantly, close to SNARE-alone levels.
source: When we used purified C2AB bearing the same mutations (C2ABR398Q, R399Q) both the fusion rate and the mean pore conductance decreased significantly, close to SNARE-alone levels (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Binding of Syt1 to calcium, PI(4,5)P2, and likely SNAREs are essential for its function in dilating SNARE-induced fusion pores.
source: Together, these results indicate that binding of Syt1 to calcium, PI(4,5)P2, and likely SNAREs, which are all crucial for Syt1's role in evoked neurotransmitter release (Brunger et al., 2018a; Chapman, 2008), are also essential for its function in dilating SNARE-induced fusion pores.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The calcium concentration at which the transition in free energy profiles occurs (~20 μM) is consistent with the known calcium binding affinity of Syt1.
source: The calcium concentration at which this transition occurs (~20 μM) is consistent with the known calcium binding affinity of Syt1 (Ma et al., 2017; Pérez-Lara et al., 2016; Bai et al., 2004b; Radhakrishnan et al., 2009; Davis et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data, supported by citations to previous work on Syt1 calcium affinity.

claim: Calcium binds simultaneously to acidic phospholipids and highly conserved aspartate residues in a pocket formed by loops at the top of the beta-sandwich structure of the Syt1 C2 domains.
source: Calcium binds simultaneously to acidic phospholipids and highly conserved aspartate residues in a pocket formed by loops at the top of the beta-sandwich structure of the Syt1 C2 domains (Chapman, 2008; Shin et al., 2009; Martens and McMahon, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Hydrophobic residues at the tips of the loops flanking the calcium-binding residues in Syt1 C2A (M173 and F234) and C2B (V304 and I367) insert into the membrane as a result of calcium binding.
source: Hydrophobic residues at the tips of the loops flanking the calcium-binding residues in Syt1 C2A (M173 and F234) and C2B (V304 and I367) insert into the membrane as a result of these interactions, strengthening membrane binding of C2 domains (Chapman, 2008; Ma et al., 2017; Chapman and Davis, 1998) while causing a reorientation of the C2 domains (Kuo et al., 2011; Herrick et al., 2006; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The membrane insertion of hydrophobic residues contributes to the triggering of release.
source: The membrane insertion of these hydrophobic residues contributes to the triggering of release (Lynch et al., 2008; Martens et al., 2007; Hui et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The membrane penetration deficient 4A mutant was non-functional, having no discernible effect on pore dilation or fusion rate when compared to the assay without Syt1.
source: In the nanodisc-cell fusion assay, the membrane penetration deficient 4A mutant was non-functional, having no discernible effect on pore dilation or fusion rate when compared to the assay without Syt1, other than a slight reduction in the fusion rate in the absence of PI(4,5)P2 (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: The 4W mutant which binds the membrane more avidly essentially behaved like the wild-type C2AB, with the exception that the pore dilation ability of the 4W mutant was less dependent on the presence of PI(4,5)P2.
source: By contrast, the 4W mutant which binds the membrane more avidly essentially behaved like the wild-type C2AB, with the exception that the pore dilation ability of the 4W mutant was less dependent on the presence of PI(4,5)P2 (Figure 5C and see Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Appendix 1—figure 7.

claim: Calcium-induced membrane penetration of Syt1 C2 domains is required for pore expansion by Syt1.
source: Thus, calcium-induced membrane penetration of Syt1 C2 domains is required for pore expansion by Syt1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments with 4A and 4W mutants.

claim: The model predicts a ~1.4-fold increase of pore radius to ~1.3 nm, or a ~2.3-fold increase in conductance when Ca2+ is introduced at high saturating concentrations, close to the experimentally measured ~2.2-fold increase.
source: When Ca2+ is introduced at high saturating concentrations, the model predicts a ~1.4-fold increase of pore radius to ~1.3 nm, or a ~2.3-fold increase in conductance, close to the experimentally measured ~2.2-fold increase (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a prediction from the mathematical model that matches experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The SNARE-C2B complex acts as a calcium-triggered mechanical lever that enlarges the fusion pore in cooperation with entropic forces generated by SNARE complexes.
source: In summary, our model suggests a mechanism in which the SNARE-C2B complex is a calcium-triggered mechanical lever that enlarges the fusion pore in cooperation with entropic forces generated by SNARE complexes (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical modeling shown in Figure 6E.

claim: On addition of Ca2+, the C2B domain rotates and inserts its calcium binding loops into the membrane, tilting the SNARE complex so that it pushes the membrane surfaces further apart in a lever action.
source: On addition of Ca2+, the C2B domain rotates and inserts its calcium binding loops into the membrane, tilting the SNARE complex so that it pushes the membrane surfaces further apart in a lever action.
evidence: This is a mechanism proposed based on the mathematical model.

claim: Fusion pore expansion can be energetically one of the costliest stages among different stages of membrane fusion.
source: Among different stages of membrane fusion, pore expansion can be energetically one of the costliest (Jackson, 2009; Cohen and Melikyan, 2004; Chizmadzhev et al., 1995; Ryham et al., 2013; Nanavati et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Fusion pores connecting protein-free lipid bilayers fluctuate, flicker open-closed, and eventually reseal unless external energy is supplied in the form of membrane tension.
source: Consistent with this notion, fusion pores connecting protein-free lipid bilayers fluctuate, flicker open-closed, and eventually reseal unless external energy is supplied in the form of membrane tension (Chanturiya et al., 1997), while the initial fusion pore during biological membrane fusion is a metastable structure whose dynamics are regulated by cellular processes (Sharma and Lindau, 2018; Chang et al., 2017; Alabi and Tsien, 2013; Collins et al., 2016; Fulop et al., 2005; Staal et al., 2004; D'Agostino et al., 2018; Doreian et al., 2009; Barg et al., 2002; Hanna et al., 2009; MacDonald et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Before membrane fusion, Syt1 was proposed to regulate membrane apposition by preventing fusion pore opening at low calcium by maintaining the membranes >5–8 nm apart, halting complete SNARE zippering.
source: Before membrane fusion, Syt1 was proposed to regulate membrane apposition (Rothman et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2018; van den Bogaart et al., 2011; Seven et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2014), preventing fusion pore opening at low calcium by maintaining the membranes >5–8 nm apart, halting complete SNARE zippering.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Upon calcium binding to Syt1, the intermembrane distance is reduced to <5 nm, sufficient for SNAREs to complete their zippering and initiate fusion.
source: Upon calcium binding to Syt1, this distance is reduced to <5 nm (Chang et al., 2018), sufficient for SNAREs to complete their zippering and initiate fusion.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Membrane tension promotes fusion pore dilation during exocytosis, often through cytoskeleton-plasma membrane interactions.
source: First, membrane tension promotes fusion pore dilation during exocytosis, often through cytoskeleton-plasma membrane interactions (Bretou et al., 2014; Kozlov and Chernomordik, 2015; Wen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Neuronal/exocytic SNARE proteins promote fusion pore dilation by providing entropic forces due to molecular crowding at the pore's waist.
source: Second, neuronal/exocytic SNARE proteins promote fusion pore dilation by providing entropic forces due to molecular crowding at the pore's waist (Wu et al., 2017b), consistent with the observation that increased SNARE availability results in larger, or faster expanding pores (Bao et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2017b; Acuna et al., 2014; Guček et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: During yeast vacuole-vacuole fusion, increased fusogen volume has been suggested as a mechanism that stabilizes fusion pores.
source: Third, during yeast vacuole-vacuole fusion, increased fusogen volume has been suggested as a mechanism that stabilizes fusion pores (D'Agostino et al., 2018; D'Agostino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Previous reconstituted single-pore measurements found Syt1 and calcium promoted expansion of SNARE-mediated fusion pores.
source: Previous reconstituted single-pore measurements by Lai et al., 2013 and Das et al., 2020 found Syt1 and calcium promoted expansion of SNARE-mediated fusion pores.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Syt1 has roles in both fusion pore formation and dilation, consistent with studies in secretory cells and in previous reconstitutions.
source: Here, we found that Syt1 has roles in both fusion pore formation and dilation, consistent with studies in secretory cells (Wang et al., 2006; Lynch et al., 2008) and in previous reconstitutions (Lai et al., 2013; Das et al., 2020), and we focused on pore dilation mechanisms.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Syt1 promotes expansion of SNARE-induced fusion pores in a calcium- and acidic lipid-dependent manner.
source: Syt1 promotes expansion of SNARE-induced fusion pores in a calcium- and acidic lipid-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: When PI(4,5)P2 is present, increasing free Ca2+ leads to pores with larger mean open-pore conductance.
source: When PI(4,5)P2 is present, increasing free Ca2+ leads to pores with larger mean open-pore conductance.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study.

claim: Fusion pore expansion by Syt1 likely relies on Syt1's interactions with the neuronal SNARE complex.
source: Fusion pore expansion by Syt1 also likely relies on Syt1's interactions with the neuronal SNARE complex, because when we used C2AB domains with mutations (R398Q,R399Q) designed to disrupt the 'primary' interaction interface with the SNARE complex (Zhou et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2017), the pore dilation function of Syt1 C2AB was largely reduced (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an inference from experimental data with mutants shown in Figure 3.

claim: The major contribution of Syt1 to pore dilation is through its mechanical modulation of the fusion pore shape.
source: A mathematical model suggests the major contribution of Syt1 to pore dilation is through its mechanical modulation of the fusion pore shape.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical modeling.

claim: Syt-SNARE complexes introduce non-local constraints on the fusion pore shape, making larger pores more energetically favorable.
source: Syt-SNARE complexes introduce non-local constraints on the fusion pore shape, making larger pores more energetically favorable.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical modeling.

claim: Calcium binding to isolated Syt1 C2 domains leads to insertion of the hydrophobic residues at the tips of both of the calcium-binding loops into the membrane.
source: Previous work showed calcium binding to isolated Syt1 C2 domains leads to insertion of the hydrophobic residues at the tips of both of the the calcium-binding loops into the membrane (Chapman, 2008; Herrick et al., 2006; Kuo et al., 2009; Bradberry et al., 2019) (however, see Bykhovskaia, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In the presence of PI(4,5)P2, calcium-bound C2B assumes a conformation in which its long axis is tilted with respect to the membrane normal.
source: In the presence of PI(4,5)P2, calcium-bound C2B assumes a conformation in which its long axis is tilted with respect to the membrane normal, as it interacts with the membrane simultaneously through its calcium binding loops and the polybasic patch (K324-327) bound to PI(4,5)P2 (Kuo et al., 2011; Pérez-Lara et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: C2B binds the t-SNAREs Stx1 and SNAP25, with its long axis parallel to the SNARE bundle, in a calcium-independent manner.
source: When present, C2B also binds the t-SNAREs Stx1 and SNAP25, with its long axis parallel to the SNARE bundle, in a calcium-independent manner (Zhou et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: At low, resting amounts of calcium, the calcium-free SNARE-C2B complex is expected to lie parallel to the membrane.
source: At low, resting amounts of calcium, the calcium-free SNARE-C2B complex is therefore expected to lie parallel to the membrane, with the C2B domain simultaneously interacting with target membrane acidic lipids and the SNARE complex (Zhou et al., 2015; Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on previous structural work and shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the presence of high calcium, the calcium-bound C2B domain will tend to reorient such that its hydrophobic top loops insert into the target membrane, resulting in a tilting of the SNARE complex of ~15 degrees.
source: By contrast, in the presence of high calcium, the calcium-bound C2B domain will tend to reorient such that its hydrophobic top loops insert into the target membrane, resulting in a tilting of the SNARE complex of ~15 degrees, which alters the pore shape (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference from the mathematical model shown in Figure 6.

claim: The resultant pore size increase quantitatively accounts for the conductance increase in the presence of Syt1, and its requirements for intact calcium- and SNARE-binding regions on C2B.
source: The resultant pore size increase quantitatively accounts for the conductance increase in the presence of Syt1, and its requirements for intact calcium- and SNARE-binding regions on C2B.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the mathematical model with experimental data.

claim: Regulation of the fusion pore shape including interbilayer distance may be a general mechanism to stabilize fusion pores against re-closure.
source: In addition, regulation of the fusion pore shape including interbilayer distance may be a general mechanism to stabilize fusion pores against re-closure, as a similar mechanism was observed during yeast vacuole-vacuole fusion (D'Agostino et al., 2018; D'Agostino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation based on comparison with previous work on yeast vacuole fusion.

claim: The correlation between the curvature-generation ability of the Syt1 mutants and pore expansion was not strong, with the 4W mutant with enhanced membrane tubulation activity having a similar effect as wild-type C2AB.
source: By contrast, here the correlation between the curvature-generation ability of the mutants and pore expansion was not strong, with the 4W mutant with enhanced membrane tubulation activity (Lynch et al., 2008; Martens et al., 2007) having a similar effect as wild-type C2AB.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Modeling supported the idea that curvature-generation by Syt1 membrane penetration is not needed to explain how Syt1 promotes pore expansion.
source: Modeling supported the idea that curvature-generation by Syt1 membrane penetration is not needed to explain how Syt1 promotes pore expansion.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical modeling.

claim: Pore expansion rate increases with increasing [Ca2+]free, from ~3–12 nS/s at low calcium (0–30 μM), to 20–25 nS/s at high calcium (40–100 μM).
source: We found pore expansion rate increases with increasing [Ca2+]free, with a similar dependence on calcium as the mean open-pore conductance (Figure 4A,D), from ~3–12 nS/s at low calcium (0–30 μM), to 20–25 nS/s at high calcium (40–100 μM).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4A,D.

claim: In horse eosinophils stimulated by intracellular application of GTP-γ-S, pores were found to expand, on average, at 19 nS/s, 40 nS/s, and 89 nS/s at low (<10 nM), 1.5 μM, and 10 μM Ca2+, respectively.
source: In horse eosinophils stimulated by intracellular application of GTP-γ-S, pores were found to expand, on average, at 19 nS/s, 40 nS/s, and 89 nS/s at low (<10 nM), 1.5 μM, and 10 μM Ca2+, respectively (Hartmann and Lindau, 1995), consistent with a later study (Scepek, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Pore expansion rates were 5–10 nS/s for rat mast cells, with higher rates at high calcium.
source: Pore expansion rates were 5–10 nS/s for rat mast cells, with higher rates at high calcium (Fernández-Chacón and Alvarez de Toledo, 1995), and varied from 15 to 50 nS/s for bovine chromaffin cells (Fang et al., 2008; Berberian et al., 2009; Dernick et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: During exocytosis, fusion pore fluctuations increase with intracellular calcium.
source: Our findings also recapitulate the observation that during exocytosis, fusion pore fluctuations increase with intracellular calcium (Zhou et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The maximal rates of secretion measured in neurons or neuroendocrine chromaffin cells is due to the rapid fusion of a pool of docked and primed vesicles called the readily releasable pool (RRP).
source: Most importantly, the maximal rates of secretion measured in neurons or neuroendocrine chromaffin cells is due to the rapid fusion of a pool of docked and primed vesicles called the readily releasable pool (RRP) (Kaeser and Regehr, 2017; Sørensen, 2004; Rizzoli and Betz, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Vesicles acquire fusion-competence at low, resting calcium levels (≲0.1 μM).
source: Vesicles acquire fusion-competence at low, resting calcium levels (≲0.1 μM).
evidence: This is established knowledge about vesicle priming.

claim: Docking (~30 s) and priming (~10 s) are much slower events than fusion from the RRP.
source: Docking (~30 s) and priming (~10 s) are much slower events (Kaeser and Regehr, 2017; Sørensen, 2004) and require tethering and priming factors such as Munc13 and Munc18 (Brunger et al., 2018a; Rizo, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The finding that fusion pore dilation is calcium sensitive suggests that the pore size, expansion rate, and duration can be modulated by calcium dynamics.
source: The finding that fusion pore dilation is calcium sensitive suggests that the pore size, expansion rate, and duration can be modulated by calcium dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Weak stimulations that result in brief calcium transients would be more likely to lead to small fusion pores and slow release, and strong stimulations would conversely result in larger and faster dilating pores.
source: Thus, weak stimulations that result in brief calcium transients would be more likely to lead to small fusion pores and slow release, and strong stimulations would conversely result in larger and faster dilating pores.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: This behavior is observed in neurons and in neuroendocrine cells.
source: This behavior is indeed observed in neurons (Pawlu et al., 2004), and in neuroendocrine cells (Fulop et al., 2005; Cárdenas and Marengo, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.
